opening_message:
Ticket 1: Edward Fleming (employee ID E042) requests write access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E042.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Payroll Specialist
  - employment type: full_time
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: Edward Fleming (E042) is a full-time Payroll Specialist. Requested write access to Source Code. Full-time employees may have up to write; write is within policy. Recommend granting write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Payroll Specialist
  - employment type: contractor
  - security training: basic
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security record for Edward Fleming (E042): contractor with basic security training (note: differs from prior team note listing full_time; Security DB is authoritative). Contractors may have read, or write only with advanced training. Requested write to Source Code exceeds max for this employee, so recommend granting read.
reason: Edward Fleming (E042) requested write access to Source Code. Security DB (authoritative) lists him as a contractor with basic security training. Contractors may have read, or write only with advanced security training. Since he has only basic training, the maximum permitted access is read, so the requested write exceeds policy and I grant the maximum of read.

content.text:
I need to reconcile the conflicting notes. The Security note says the Security DB is authoritative: Edward Fleming is a contractor with basic security training. Contractors may have read, or write only with advanced training. Since basic training, max is read. Requested write exceeds max, so grant read (the maximum).

The HR note says full_time Payroll Specialist, which would allow write (and even admin since role owns... wait, Payroll Specialist owns Payroll, not Source Code, so admin not applicable anyway). But Security DB is authoritative per the note.

So decision: read for Source Code.

Let me submit.
